title: Commercial Strip Mall FDC / Standpipe Supply

hoses: Supply line from hydrant to Engine 181 intake
FDC Supply Line A: 100 ft of 2½-inch hose from Engine 181 discharge to building FDC
FDC Supply Line B: 100 ft of 2½-inch hose from Engine 181 discharge to building FDC
Interior attack line: 150 ft of 2½-inch hose from standpipe outlet to nozzle
appliances: Building FDC / standpipe system; use losses stated in each problem

problems.title: Known Standpipe Flow With Unknown Sprinkler Flow
problems.question: Engine 181 is supplying one interior standpipe attack line using a 1⅛-inch smooth bore nozzle at 50 PSI. A separate sprinkler FDC support line is connected, but the sprinkler system flowing GPM is unknown. Using smooth-bore flow = 29.7 × diameter² × √NP, and not adding unknown sprinkler flow as a known demand, what known standpipe attack flow should be used for the operation?
formulaBreakdown: Sprinkler FDC flow is unknown, so do not add an assumed sprinkler GPM.
problems.instructorExplanation: Calculate only the known standpipe attack flow; do not invent a sprinkler GPM value.
problems.explainMistake: Unknown sprinkler flow is not a known demand to add to the standpipe attack flow.

problems.title: FDC Supply Line Friction Loss
problems.question: The building FDC is supplied by two equal 100 ft 2½-inch lines. The known standpipe attack flow is 265 GPM, while the separate sprinkler support flow is unknown and excluded. Split the known standpipe flow equally between the two FDC supply lines. Using FL = C × (GPM/100)² × (length/100), with C = 2, what is the friction loss in each FDC supply line?
formulaBreakdown: Flow per equal FDC line = 265 ÷ 2 = 132.5 GPM.
problems.instructorExplanation: The two equal FDC lines split the known standpipe flow, so each carries 132.5 GPM.
problems.explainMistake: Do not calculate each FDC supply line at the full 265 GPM.

problems.title: Sixth-Floor Standpipe Elevation
problems.question: An interior standpipe attack is operating on the 6th floor. For this training problem, use height = (floor number - 1) × 10 ft and elevation pressure = height × 0.5 PSI/ft. What elevation pressure must be added?
formulaBreakdown: 6th floor is 5 floors above the 1st floor.
problems.instructorExplanation: This question asks only for the elevation component, not standpipe system loss or pump discharge pressure.
problems.explainMistake: Do not label the 25 PSI result as system loss; it is elevation pressure.

problems.title: Total Pump Discharge Pressure
problems.question: Engine 181 is supplying a grade-level standpipe attack through two equal 100 ft 2½-inch FDC supply lines. The known attack flow is 265 GPM; split that flow equally between the two FDC supply lines. The interior attack line is 150 ft of 2½-inch hose flowing 265 GPM through a 1⅛-inch smooth bore at 50 PSI. For this training scenario, assume 25 PSI FDC/standpipe system loss and no elevation. What pump discharge pressure should be set?
formulaBreakdown: Interior attack-line FL = 2 × (265/100)^2 × 1.5 ≈ 21 PSI, rounded to 20 PSI.
problems.instructorExplanation: This problem explicitly assumes a 25 PSI FDC/standpipe system loss. It is a scenario value, not a universal standpipe loss.
problems.explainMistake: Include the full pressure path: FDC hose loss, interior hose loss, nozzle pressure, and the loss stated by the scenario.

problems.title: Elevated Sprinkler FDC Support Pressure
problems.question: For this sprinkler-only FDC training problem, the sprinkler system flowing GPM is unknown. Use the stated scenario rule: PDP = 150 PSI base + elevation pressure. Elevation pressure = (floor number - 1) × 10 ft × 0.5 PSI/ft. The sprinkler area being supported is on the 4th floor. No flow-based friction loss or other losses are used. What pump discharge pressure should be set?
formulaBreakdown: Sprinkler flowing GPM is unknown, so no flow-based friction loss is calculated.
problems.instructorExplanation: This is a stated training assumption, not a universal department or code rule. Follow the scenario values shown.
problems.explainMistake: Do not invent sprinkler flow, and do not treat the 150 PSI scenario base as a universal setting for every system.
